old:
Gross Domestic Product — the total monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given year: the primary measure of economic activity.

Actual growth is a rise in real GDP — producing more than last year. Potential growth is a rise in productive capacity — what the economy could produce at full employment.
new:
Gross Domestic Product — the total monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given year: the primary measure of economic activity.

Actual growth is a rise in real GDP — producing more than last year.

Potential growth is a rise in productive capacity — what the economy could produce at full employment.

old:
Nominal GDP is measured at current prices; real GDP is adjusted for inflation, showing the true change in the volume of output — the measure of growth (value vs volume). GDP per capita divides real GDP by population — the better guide to average living standards.

GNI — GDP plus net income from abroad, such as profits sent home by citizens overseas minus income flowing out to foreign owners.
new:
Nominal GDP is measured at current prices; real GDP is adjusted for inflation, showing the true change in the volume of output — the measure of growth (value vs volume).

GDP per capita divides real GDP by population — the better guide to average living standards.

GNI — GDP plus net income from abroad, such as profits sent home by citizens overseas minus income flowing out to foreign owners.

old:
GDP per capita masks inequality; excludes unpaid work, leisure and environmental quality; counts welfare-reducing 'bads' like pollution clean-up; struggles with quality improvements; and misses the informal economy.

Hence the spec's interest in national wellbeing: the UK measures subjective happiness alongside GDP, and rising real incomes raise reported happiness only weakly beyond a point.
new:
• GDP per capita masks inequality.
  • It excludes unpaid work, leisure and environmental quality.
  • It counts welfare-reducing 'bads' like pollution clean-up.
  • It struggles with quality improvements.
  • It misses the informal economy.

Hence the interest in national wellbeing: the UK measures subjective happiness alongside GDP, and rising real incomes raise reported happiness only weakly beyond a point.

old:
Inflation — a sustained increase in the general/average price level of goods and services in an economy.

Deflation — a sustained decrease in the general price level: a negative inflation rate. Disinflation — a decrease in the rate of inflation: prices still rising, but more slowly.
new:
Inflation — a sustained increase in the general/average price level of goods and services in an economy.

Deflation — a sustained decrease in the general price level: a negative inflation rate.

Disinflation — a decrease in the rate of inflation: prices still rising, but more slowly.

old:
CPI: 2023 = 100; 2024 = 504 ÷ 480 × 100 = 105; 2025 = 524.16 ÷ 480 × 100 = 109.2

Inflation 2024 = (105 − 100) ÷ 100 × 100 = 5%

Inflation 2025 = (109.2 − 105) ÷ 105 × 100 = 4%

Inflation fell yet the basket still costs more — disinflation, not deflation. Each year's rate is measured against the previous year's index, not the base year.
new:
CPI 2023 = 100 (the base year)

CPI 2024 = 504 ÷ 480 × 100 = 105

CPI 2025 = 524.16 ÷ 480 × 100 = 109.2

Inflation 2024 = (105 − 100) ÷ 100 × 100 = 5%

Inflation 2025 = (109.2 − 105) ÷ 105 × 100 = 4%

Inflation fell yet the basket still costs more — disinflation, not deflation. Each year's rate is measured against the previous year's index, not the base year.

old: Explain the three causes of inflation in the Edexcel specification.
new: Explain the three causes of inflation.

old:
Demand-pull — anything raising C, I, G or X−M shifts AD right and pulls the price level up. Cost-push — higher production costs (commodity prices, wages, indirect taxes, a weaker currency) shift SRAS left, raising prices while cutting output.

Money supply growth — excessive growth (e.g. quantitative easing) fuels both: cheaper borrowing boosts spending, and a depreciating currency raises import costs. A wage-price spiral can then sustain inflation after the original cause fades.
new:
Demand-pull — anything raising C, I, G or X−M shifts AD right and pulls the price level up.

Cost-push — higher production costs (commodity prices, wages, indirect taxes, a weaker currency) shift SRAS left, raising prices while cutting output.

Money supply growth — excessive growth (e.g. quantitative easing) fuels both: cheaper borrowing boosts spending, and a depreciating currency raises import costs.

A wage-price spiral can then sustain inflation after the original cause fades.

old:
Consumers — real incomes and the value of savings erode, hitting living standards. Firms — uncertainty discourages investment, higher inflation than trading partners erodes international competitiveness, and menu costs mount.

Government — index-linked pensions and benefits cost more, widening the deficit. Workers — real wages fall unless pay keeps pace, prompting the wage demands that can spiral.
new:
• Consumers — real incomes and the value of savings erode, hitting living standards.
  • Firms — uncertainty discourages investment, higher inflation than trading partners erodes international competitiveness, and menu costs mount.
  • Government — index-linked pensions and benefits cost more, widening the deficit.
  • Workers — real wages fall unless pay keeps pace, prompting the wage demands that can spiral.

old:
Unemployed — an individual of working age who is without work, but is willing and able to work, and is actively seeking employment.

Labour force — those in employment plus the unemployed actively seeking work. Economically inactive — working-age people not seeking work: full-time students, early retirees, the long-term sick, discouraged workers.
new:
Unemployed — an individual of working age who is without work, but is willing and able to work, and is actively seeking employment.

Labour force — those in employment plus the unemployed actively seeking work.

Economically inactive — working-age people not seeking work: full-time students, early retirees, the long-term sick, discouraged workers.

old:
Individuals — lower incomes and living standards, skills erode, health suffers. Government and society — lower tax revenue and higher welfare spending widen the deficit; social costs rise. Firms — weaker sales, though a larger labour pool can lower hiring costs.

Migration cuts unemployment where migrants fill shortages, and migrants' spending creates jobs; competition can raise unemployment in particular low-skilled sectors. Skills determine who escapes structural unemployment.
new:
• Individuals — lower incomes and living standards, skills erode, health suffers.
  • Government and society — lower tax revenue and higher welfare spending widen the deficit; social costs rise.
  • Firms — weaker sales, though a larger labour pool can lower hiring costs.

Migration cuts unemployment where migrants fill shortages, and migrants' spending creates jobs; competition can raise unemployment in particular low-skilled sectors.

Skills determine who escapes structural unemployment.

old:
Balance of payments — a record of all financial transactions between a country and the rest of the world. It must always balance: total credits equal total debits.

Current account — trade and income flows. Capital account — capital transfers and non-produced assets (small, often ignored). Financial account — cross-border investment flows (FDI, portfolio investment, reserves), which finance the current account balance.
new:
Balance of payments — a record of all financial transactions between a country and the rest of the world. It must always balance: total credits equal total debits.

  • Current account — trade and income flows.
  • Capital account — capital transfers and non-produced assets (small, often ignored).
  • Financial account — cross-border investment flows (FDI, portfolio investment, reserves), which finance the current account balance.

old:
Causes: high consumer spending and low saving pulling in imports; weak competitiveness and low productivity; a strong currency; slowdown in export markets; structural issues such as deindustrialisation.

Corrections trade off against other objectives — cutting demand through fiscal or monetary tightening slows growth and raises unemployment; supply-side improvement works but slowly and at a cost. Economies are interconnected through trade, so one country's deficit is another's surplus.
new:
Causes:

  • High consumer spending and low saving pulling in imports.
  • Weak competitiveness and low productivity.
  • A strong currency.
  • Slowdown in export markets.
  • Structural issues such as deindustrialisation.

Corrections trade off against other objectives — cutting demand through fiscal or monetary tightening slows growth and raises unemployment; supply-side improvement works but slowly and at a cost.

Economies are interconnected through trade, so one country's deficit is another's surplus.

old: C — consumption: household spending on goods and services. I — investment: firms' spending on capital goods. G — government spending on state-provided goods and services, excluding transfer payments such as benefits. (X − M) — exports minus imports.
new:
• C — consumption: household spending on goods and services.
  • I — investment: firms' spending on capital goods.
  • G — government spending on state-provided goods and services, excluding transfer payments such as benefits.
  • (X − M) — exports minus imports.

old:
AD = 1,200 + 280 + 500 + (640 − 660) = £1,960bn

Net trade is negative (−£20bn) because imports exceed exports, so it is subtracted. The shares match the UK pattern: consumption 61%, government 26%, investment 14%, net trade −1%.

old:
MPC — the proportion of an increase in disposable income that is spent on consumption. MPS — the proportion of an increase in disposable income that is saved.

If a household spends £80 of an extra £100, the MPC is 0.8. A rise in the MPC means a fall in the MPS — every extra pound is either spent or saved.
new:
MPC — the proportion of an increase in disposable income that is spent on consumption.

MPS — the proportion of an increase in disposable income that is saved.

If a household spends £80 of an extra £100, the MPC is 0.8. A rise in the MPC means a fall in the MPS — every extra pound is either spent or saved.

old:
Gross investment — total spending on capital goods. Net investment — gross investment minus depreciation: the true addition to the capital stock, which is what raises productive potential.

Depreciation — the loss of value of capital goods over time due to wear and tear, obsolescence, or other factors. A firm spending £1m on machinery while £200,000 of capital wears out makes £800,000 of net investment.
new:
Gross investment — total spending on capital goods.

Net investment — gross investment minus depreciation: the true addition to the capital stock, which is what raises productive potential.

Depreciation — the loss of value of capital goods over time due to wear and tear, obsolescence, or other factors.

A firm spending £1m on machinery while £200,000 of capital wears out makes £800,000 of net investment.

old: List the influences on investment in the Edexcel specification.
new: List the influences on investment.

old:
The trade cycle — spending rises automatically in downturns as welfare claims grow, and falls in booms.

Fiscal policy — discretionary choices: expansionary policy raises G (infrastructure, education) to boost AD, growth and jobs; contractionary policy cuts G to cool inflation or close a deficit. Political priorities and demographics (an ageing population) shape the mix.
new:
The trade cycle — spending rises automatically in downturns as welfare claims grow, and falls in booms.

Fiscal policy — discretionary choices:

  • Expansionary policy raises G (infrastructure, education) to boost AD, growth and jobs.
  • Contractionary policy cuts G to cool inflation or close a deficit.

Political priorities and demographics (an ageing population) shape the mix.

old:
Net trade — exports minus imports (X − M). A surplus (X > M) adds to aggregate demand; a deficit (X < M) subtracts from it.

Influences: real incomes at home and abroad, exchange rates, the state of the world economy, the degree of protectionism, and non-price factors such as quality, branding and innovation.
new:
Net trade — exports minus imports (X − M).

A surplus (X > M) adds to aggregate demand; a deficit (X < M) subtracts from it.

Influences:

  • Real incomes at home and abroad.
  • Exchange rates.
  • The state of the world economy.
  • The degree of protectionism.
  • Non-price factors such as quality, branding and innovation.

old:
Real incomes — rising domestic incomes pull in imports (worsening); rising foreign incomes lift exports (improving). World economy — global growth lifts export demand, and for an open economy like the UK it is often the most important short-run driver.

Protectionism — tariffs and quotas cut imports, but invite retaliation against exports and raise prices at home. Non-price competitiveness — quality, branding and innovation decide who wins the trade that prices don't.
new:
• Real incomes — rising domestic incomes pull in imports (worsening); rising foreign incomes lift exports (improving).
  • World economy — global growth lifts export demand, and for an open economy like the UK it is often the most important short-run driver.
  • Protectionism — tariffs and quotas cut imports, but invite retaliation against exports and raise prices at home.
  • Non-price competitiveness — quality, branding and innovation decide who wins the trade that prices don't.

old:
SRAS shows what firms will produce at different price levels while at least one factor is fixed. LRAS shows what the economy can produce at maximum potential — its productive capacity.

In the long run the economy tends towards the LRAS level of output; SRAS shocks are temporary adjustments around that trend. Long-run growth is an outward shift of LRAS.
new:
SRAS shows what firms will produce at different price levels while at least one factor is fixed.

LRAS shows what the economy can produce at maximum potential — its productive capacity.

In the long run the economy tends towards the LRAS level of output; SRAS shocks are temporary adjustments around that trend. Long-run growth is an outward shift of LRAS.

old: State the factors that shift SRAS in the Edexcel specification.
new: State the factors that shift SRAS.

old:
Three cost factors: changes in costs of raw materials and energy, changes in exchange rates and changes in tax rates (indirect taxes raise costs; subsidies work in reverse).

All operate through production costs — falling costs shift SRAS right, rising costs shift it left. Supply shocks such as natural disasters or sudden oil-price moves act the same way.
new:
Three cost factors:

  • Changes in costs of raw materials and energy.
  • Changes in exchange rates.
  • Changes in tax rates (indirect taxes raise costs; subsidies work in reverse).

All operate through production costs — falling costs shift SRAS right, rising costs shift it left.

Supply shocks such as natural disasters or sudden oil-price moves act the same way.

old: Keynesians argue the economy can sit below full employment for a long time, so the curve is L-shaped with three phases: perfectly elastic at low output, where spare capacity lets firms expand without raising prices; upward sloping as resources grow scarcer and rising costs are passed on; and vertical at full capacity Yfe, where extra demand only raises prices.
new:
Keynesians argue the economy can sit below full employment for a long time, so the curve is L-shaped with three phases:

  • Perfectly elastic at low output, where spare capacity lets firms expand without raising prices.
  • Upward sloping as resources grow scarcer and rising costs are passed on.
  • Vertical at full capacity Yfe, where extra demand only raises prices.
